headline: Heat-bath mixing in the SK spin glass is fast below β = 1, takes n^(2/3) at β = 1, and slows sharply above it.
scope: It covers zero-field SK heat-bath dynamics, in probability over the random strengths. The critical universality results are at β = 1 only.
plain: The Sherrington–Kirkpatrick model is a classic random magnet with n interacting spins. The papers study how fast a natural random update process reaches equilibrium. They claim fast mixing with a sharp cutoff at high temperature and a time of about n^(2/3) at the critical point. Below the critical temperature, typical starts take much longer.
doesNot: This does not give a cutoff or a leading constant at the critical point.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: David Sherrington and Scott Kirkpatrick, the infinite-range spin glass
scorecard.significanceWhy: It covers the whole high-temperature phase and fixes the critical mixing exponent for a central spin-glass model.

explanation:
Take n tiny magnets, called spins, each pointing up or down. Every pair is joined by a random strength, positive or negative. This is the Sherrington–Kirkpatrick (SK) model, introduced in 1975[1]. A number β, the inverse temperature, sets how strongly the spins feel those pulls. At β = 1 the model changes phase. Below 1 it behaves like a hot, loose system. Above 1 it becomes a spin glass, frozen in a rugged landscape.

Now let the spins move. Each spin carries a clock that rings on average once per time unit. When it rings, the spin is redrawn at random, given its neighbors. This is heat-bath dynamics. The mixing time is how long it takes, from the worst start, to look like a typical equilibrium sample.

The papers find three regimes. Take n = 1,000 spins. At β = 1, the mixing time grows like n^(2/3), here about 100 time units. That is about 100,000 single-spin updates, since each time unit has n of them. Below β = 1, mixing takes only about log n time units, here about 6.9 times a constant. Above β = 1, typical starts take time that grows faster than any power of n.

Earlier proofs covered only part of the hot phase. Bauerschmidt and Bodineau proved a key inequality for β below 1/4[3]. Others turned results like this into fast mixing in that range. Later work pushed the range up to 1/2, and slightly past it at zero field[4]. None of these bounds reach β = 1 by taking a limit[5]. Physicists had seen the n^(2/3) scale in simulations[2].

The spectral-gap paper proves that the dynamics stays well-mixed at every β below 1[7]. Equivalently, the equilibrium law satisfies a Poincaré inequality, a bound on how much any function can vary, that does not grow with n[6]. A second paper claims cutoff for every β below 1[8]. Cutoff means the distance from equilibrium stays near its maximum and then drops suddenly, at time log n / (2λ(β)) for an explicit rate λ(β).

At β = 1, one paper proves that typical equilibrium starts are still far from equilibrium before time n^(2/3)[12]. The critical mixing paper claims the matching upper bound, so the mixing time is n^(2/3 + o(1))[10]. The o(1) means the exponent is right up to any small slack. It does not claim a cutoff or a leading constant[11]. The obstacle at β = 1 is that equilibrium fluctuations are much larger than for independent spins[19]. Every bound must hold from every start and for every test function.

Above β = 1, one paper proves a barrier for typical starts. Starting from a sampled equilibrium state, the dynamics is still far from equilibrium at time exp(n^(1/10000))[13]. That bound only matters for huge n. For a million spins it is about 2.72 time units. Another paper claims an upper bound for typical starts, below exp(n) by a tiny power[14].

Two more papers look at β = 1 more closely. They scale time by n^(2/3) and multiply the average spin autocorrelation by n^(1/3)[16]. With n = 1,000 that factor is 10. The limit is the same for Gaussian and ±1 strengths[9]. It stays random from sample to sample[15]. One paper starts from independent fair spins, a sudden cooling called a quench[18]. Its limit relaxes to the equilibrium one over long waiting times[17].

How sure is this? Lean, a computer proof checker, has formal versions of several pieces. They include the spectral gap for every β below 1, and cutoff for β below 1/2. At β = 1, Lean bounds the mixing time between n^(2/3−ε) and e^(εn), so the matching upper bound is not in it. It also covers the β > 1 barrier. The universality papers and the β > 1 upper bound are not covered. No specialist review of these papers has been published.
hypeCheck: Major if the proofs hold. Lean covers the spectral gap, cutoff below β = 1/2, critical lower bounds and the β > 1 barrier. The critical upper exponent and universality are not covered, and no specialist review is published.

glossary.meaning: n spins with independent random pairwise strengths, all pairs interacting.
A setting that scales how strongly spins feel their interactions.
A process that repeatedly redraws one spin from its correct conditional law given the others.
How long the process needs, from the worst start, to be close to equilibrium.
A rate that controls how fast averages settle; bounded away from zero means fast settling.
A sudden drop from far to near equilibrium within a short time window.
How much a spin still agrees with its earlier value after a time lag.
